As global capitals fumble after Trump's return to the White
House, PM Modi frames India's outlook with candour and clarity
OR CAPITALSACROSS the globe, Donald Trump's retum to the White House has
been marked by large disruptions in the international order. In terms of cur-
rentconflicts — especially in Ukraine and Palestine — and the broader role of the
US in the world, countries appear to be struggling to find and forge a response
to the US president's “America First” agenda, whetherin terms of tariffs, with regard to
international organisations or the strategic changes he is ushering in. In the context of
this ongoing chum — vis-a-vis NATO withinthe West, USvs China and the uncertainties
in West Asia — Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to podcaster Lex Fridman and framed
the contours of Delhi's position with candour and clarity. Two broad themes emerged:
First, in an uncertain world, India's foreign policy seeks to maximise its room for ma-
noeuvre. Second, the decline of global bodies such as the UN as well as perceived disillu-
sionment with the falloutsof globalisation have led to anintemationalism thatis rooted,
in terms of values and realpolitik, in nationalism.
PM Modi spoke at length about his friendship with Trump since the latter's first term
and praised aspects of “Amenica First”, juxtaposing it with hisown priority of “india First”.
That said, “India First” is also a statement ofan indenendent foreign policy. Intermsof the
Russia- Ukraine conflict, the PM reiterated that Indiais anactive votary for peace, and not
“neutral”. The bigideas were alsobalanced bya pragmatic iinderstancing. On Ukraine, for
example, PM Modi said: “Ukraine may hold countless discussions with their allies, but it
will bear no fruit,” until both parties in the conflict talk to each other. On China, the PM
spoke of “civilisational” ties and the imperative that disagreements tetween the twoneigh-
bours do not escalate into conflicts — his statements have been welcomed by Beijing. He
reiterated India's position on UN reforms and said the institutionis“al most irrelevant".
Foreign policy inthe age of social media and 2.4/7 news often falls victim to thesame
traps asdomestic politics. Tit-for-tat Guitragemiactiiies battte each other, usuallywith an
eye on domestic constituencies. At present, with conflicts raging and alliances shifting,
Delhihasdone well inengaging — and doing business — with allsides. The calibrated re-
action to illegal Indian migrants being deported from the USis ofa piece with this strat-
egy. India must continue to be nimblein changing cimiumstances — something thatis al-
lowed by the PM's framing. In the first few decades after Independence, India punched
well above its weight in the intemational system through non-alignment, deploying a

grade. The language of national interest allows for drawingred lines while leaving room
for negotiation. Perhaps the mandarins in Europe, panicked at Trump's retum, can take
a leaf out of India's playbook.

Policy for incentivising electronic manufacturing could help
deepen and broaden the manufacturing ecosystem
NAN ATTEMPT ® incentivise large-scale private sector investments in the coun-
try, the Union government, in 2020, launched the production linked incentive(PLI)
scheme. While the PLI scheme was launched for anumber of sectors, one segment
where significant traction has beeii visibi¢is mobite phones. As per reports, India's
mobile phone ex ports exceeded Rs25,000 crore in January, and are expected tocrossRs
18 lakh crore by the end of this fiscal year, an increase of 40 percent from last year A large
partof thishas been drivenby Apple, which throughits contract manufacturers has built
upa sizable base. In January, Apple reportedly accounted for 70 per cent of all mobile
phone shinments. In fact, its three contract manufactuwers — Foxconn, Tata Electronicsand
Pegatron — accounted for 75 per cent of all disbursements released by the govemment
under the PLI scheme bet ween 2022-23 and 2024-25. However, despite the success,
some questions have been raised over the extent of value addition in the country. Inter-
ministerial discussions inthe government are also reported to have noted thatvaluead-
dition across sectors was low, even in segments where the PLI scheme was faring well.
In a bid to increase the domestic value addition — from 15-20 per cent in some sec-
tors to around 30-40 per cent — the govemmentis reported to have finalised the con-
tours of a broader policy for electronic components’ manufacturing. The components
whichare the target ofthe scheme include display modules, sub assembly camera mod-
ules and printed circuit boards, among others. The overall outlay for the scheme, which
is expected to span six years, has been pegged at around Rs23,000crore. The incentives,
which will be paid annually, will be conditional on firms meeting investment, production
and employment goals. The schemecould help facilitate the creation of alarger domes-
fic elecinonicsecosvdem, thereby helping deenen and broaden the manufacturing ecosys-
tem in the country. An intemal assessment carried out by the govemment had earlier
estimated a “huge” demand-supply gap in the sector. Thus atieiipisioincentivise greater
private investments, boost domestic value addition, are indeed welcome. There are also
employment benefits to consider. The scheme aims to generate 91,600 jobs directly.
In the current global environment of heightened geopolitical risks, where countries
are locked in tariff and trade wars,and supply chains are being rejigged, Indiahasa unique
opportunity. It must seize the moment.

2001, a Pratichi Trust survey revealed that in
some schools, Scheduled Caste (SC) students
were forced t sit separately. In 2004, a few
newspapers carried stories on higher-caste
parents’ objections to their children eating
cooked meais prepared by the SC volunteers.
Such incidents suggest that though caste
discrimination is nota major public issue,
caste remains a reality in Bengal’'s everyday
absence of casteism per se but the invisibility
of caste in publiclife The nvibilityofcasteis
anexpression ofacadeism of adifferent kind,
which, despite being deeptyentrenched, dis-
guises itself into inconspicuous forms,
The hyper-invisibility of caste in Bengal is
an outcome of the Bhadralok's hegemonic so-
ial position. The Bhadralok, historically, is a
product of the 19th century Bengal
Renaissance. Being the earliest beneficiaries
of Westerneducatinn and modemity by virtue
of their advantageous caste position, they
ended up acquiring the hegemonic power to
define the legitimate norms of social and po-
litical behaviour. After Independence, they

emerged as the intellectual driving force of the
class politics of the Left, which de-legitimised
thelexiconofcaste in the nameof secularisa-
tion of the public sphere. As a result, though
power relations are segregated along caste
lines, sustained social dialogue on everyday
experiencesof caste remains absent, preclud-
ing the emergence of an effective and power-
fulDalit counter-culture.
Such a scenario allows the practice of dif-
ferent forms of everyday casteism, like the fre-
quent use of casteist slurs like cramar and
chotolok. The fact that most people use these
words casually, often unaware of their casteist
connotations, shows the extent of casual
casteism. Though caste riots are not frequent
in Bengal, whenever it happens, it's conve-
niently presented as a law-and-order prob-
lem. It is only recently that researchers have
Started reading caste int a forgotten chapter
of history — the merciless massacre of Dalit
refugeesin Marichjhapiin the Sundarbans,al-
legedly by police and Left cadres, in 1979.
However, the most potent form of
casteism is embedded in the persistent at-
tempts by the higher-caste-dominated power
structure 0 blockall avenues of social mobil-
ity for the lowercastes For instance, the Dalits
have remainedabysmally unaer-represented
inthe West Bengal Assembly and cabinet for
decades. Moreover the dominant disposition
towards reservation remains overwhdimingly
negative. Opposing the identification of the
OBCs based on caste, Jyoti Basu, then chief
minister, submitted before the Mandal
Commission that West Bengal had only two
castes: Rich and poor.

In 1994, the Left Front govemment grudg-
inglyimplementeda meagre five per centOBC
quota in government employment, which
was later raised & seven per cent. Currently,
the OBC quota in West Bengal is 17 per cent,
much lower than the Mandal Commission
recommendation of 27 per cent. Still, the
caste-hased stiomatisation of beneficiariesof
reservation is quite pervasive. Terms like Sonar
Chand(golden moon )and Sonar Tulco (piece
of gold) are widely used to demean the SCs
and STs (Scheduled Tribes). In 1992, Chuni
Kotal, a VidyasagarUniversity student and first
woman graduate from the Lodha tribe, died
by suicide, subjected t casteist humiliation
by oneof her professors.
in the literary and cultural worlds too,
Dalits face exclusion. Bengali Dalit literature
as amovement emerged inthe 1990s, much
laterthan its counterparts in otherpartsof the
country and is still jostling for attentioninthe
Bhadralok-dominated space. While a few
Bengali Dalit writers have gained recognition,
the readership remains limited dueto the re-
luctance of mainstream publishing houses to
publish their writings.
The invisibility of caste in West Bengalisa
complex tory woven with intricate plots and
subplots. The key to comprehending such
complexities lies in acknowledging that,
whether as villaiiis or not, the central protag-
onistsof this story are certainly the Bhadratok,
the high priests of Bengali culture.

In 2004, a few newspapers carried stories on higher-caste parents' objections to their children eating cooked meais prepared by the SC volunteers. Such incidents suggest that though caste discrimination is nota major public issue, caste remains a reality in Bengal''s everyday absence of casteism per se but the invisibility of caste in publiclife The nvibilityofcasteis anexpression ofacadeism of adifferent kind, which, despite being deeptyentrenched, disguises itself into inconspicuous forms, The hyper-invisibility of caste in Bengal is an outcome of the Bhadralok's hegemonic soial position. The Bhadralok, historically, is a product of the 19th century Bengal Renaissance. Being the earliest beneficiaries of Westerneducatinn and modemity by virtue of their advantageous caste position, they ended up acquiring the hegemonic power to define the legitimate norms of social and political behaviour. After Independence, they

emerged as the intellectual driving force of the class politics of the Left, which de-legitimised thelexiconofcaste in the nameof secularisation of the public sphere. As a result, though power relations are segregated along caste lines, sustained social dialogue on everyday experiencesof caste remains absent, precluding the emergence of an effective and power-fulDalit counter-culture. Such a scenario allows the practice of different forms of everyday casteism, like the frequent use of casteist slurs like cramar and chotolok. The fact that most people use these words casually, often unaware of their casteist connotations, shows the extent of casual casteism. Though caste riots are not frequent in Bengal, whenever it happens, it's conveniently presented as a law-and-order problem. It is only recently that researchers have Started reading caste int a forgotten chapter of history - the merciless massacre of Dalit refugeesin Marichjhapiin the Sundarbans,allegedly by police and Left cadres, in 1979. However, the most potent form of casteism is embedded in the persistent attempts by the higher-caste-dominated power structure 0 blockall avenues of social mobility for the lowercastes For instance, the Dalits have remainedabysmally unaer-represented inthe West Bengal Assembly and cabinet for decades. Moreover the dominant disposition towards reservation remains overwhdimingly negative. Opposing the identification of the OBCs based on caste, Jyoti Basu, then chief minister, submitted before the Mandal Commission that West Bengal had only two castes: Rich and poor.

In 1994, the Left Front govemment grudginglyimplementeda meagre five per centOBC quota in government employment, which was later raised & seven per cent. Currently, the OBC quota in West Bengal is 17 per cent, much lower than the Mandal Commission recommendation of 27 per cent. Still, the caste-hased stiomatisation of beneficiariesof reservation is quite pervasive. Terms like Sonar Chand(golden moon )and Sonar Tulco (piece of gold) are widely used to demean the SCs and STs (Scheduled Tribes). In 1992, Chuni Kotal, a VidyasagarUniversity student and first woman graduate from the Lodha tribe, died by suicide, subjected t casteist humiliation by oneof her professors. in the literary and cultural worlds too, Dalits face exclusion. Bengali Dalit literature as amovement emerged inthe 1990s, much laterthan its counterparts in otherpartsof the country and is still jostling for attentioninthe Bhadralok-dominated space. While a few Bengali Dalit writers have gained recognition, the readership remains limited dueto the reluctance of mainstream publishing houses to publish their writings. The invisibility of caste in West Bengalisa complex tory woven with intricate plots and subplots. The key to comprehending such complexities lies in acknowledging that, whether as villaiiis or not, the central protagonistsof this story are certainly the Bhadratok, the high priests of Bengali culture.
